items.title: Newton's biggest theorem says integration and differentiation are inverses
items.claim: Define F(x) as the area under f from 0 to x. The derivative of F is f. Define G(x) as an antiderivative of f. Then integral from a to b of f dx = G(b) - G(a). Two operations that look unrelated are inverses.

options.text: Integration (continuous summation) and differentiation (instantaneous rate) seem like different operations — but they undo each other. This is one of the most surprising and powerful results in mathematics

items.reveal:
Two parts:

FTC Part I: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).

FTC Part II: If f is continuous on [a, b] and G is any antiderivative of f (so G'(x) = f(x)), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a).

Geometric intuition for Part I: F(x) is area under the curve up to x. As x increases by a small amount dx, the area increases by approximately f(x) * dx — the height at x times the width dx. So dF/dx = f(x).

Why it's surprising:
- Differentiation computes a LOCAL rate at one point.
- Integration sums up TOTAL accumulated value across a range.
- The connection: knowing the total at every point tells you the rate; knowing the rate everywhere tells you the total.

Applications:
- Definite integrals become easy: find an antiderivative, plug in endpoints, subtract.
- Areas, volumes, work, charge, total amounts of accumulated quantities — all computable via antiderivatives.
- Differential equations: solving f' = g is equivalent to finding an antiderivative of g.

Historical: Newton (~1665) and Leibniz (~1675) both discovered it independently. It's the cornerstone of mathematical physics.

Before the FTC, calculating areas under curves (the 'quadrature problem') was a major mathematical challenge — Archimedes computed parabola areas through laborious limit arguments. After the FTC, antiderivatives reduce the problem to algebra.
items.why: Calculus has two halves that look unrelated. The fundamental theorem reveals they are inverses — the same way logarithm and exponential are inverses. This unification is the most powerful idea in elementary mathematics.

items.title: A skydiver and a feather hit terminal velocity at hugely different speeds — but the math is the same
items.claim: Drop a steel ball: terminal velocity ~150 m/s. Drop a person: ~50 m/s. Drop a feather: ~1 m/s. All fall under the same gravity. The differences come from one equation: weight equals drag.

options.text: Terminal velocity is where gravitational force (mg, downward) exactly balances drag force (proportional to v squared for high speeds, or v for low speeds); the equilibrium speed depends on mass, cross-sectional area, drag coefficient and air density
Only on the height of the fall
Drag is the same for all objects

items.reveal_title: The drag equation and limit velocities
items.reveal:
For an object falling through air, two forces:
- Gravity: mg, downward.
- Drag: at high speed, F_drag = (1/2) * rho * v^2 * C_d * A, where rho is air density, C_d is drag coefficient, A is cross-sectional area.

At terminal velocity, drag equals gravity: v_terminal = sqrt(2 * m * g / (rho * C_d * A)).

Approximate terminal velocities:
- Steel ball (cm-scale): ~150 m/s.
- Skydiver in spread-eagle: ~50 m/s.
- Skydiver in head-first dive: ~90 m/s.
- Tennis ball: ~30 m/s.
- Raindrop (1mm): ~6.5 m/s.
- Snowflake: ~0.5-1 m/s.
- Dust mote: micrometres per second.

The famous 'Galileo dropped balls from the leaning tower of Pisa' demonstrates that g is the same for all masses — but only in vacuum. In air, lighter objects with high surface area to mass ratio fall slower because of drag.

Apollo 15 (1971): astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the lunar surface (no atmosphere). They hit the ground simultaneously — Galileo confirmed live on Earth television.

Felix Baumgartner (Red Bull Stratos jump, 2012) reached supersonic terminal velocity (~377 m/s) by jumping from the stratosphere where air is thinner. He broke the sound barrier with his body.
items.why: Galileo showed all objects fall the same — in vacuum. In air, drag dominates within seconds and terminal velocity is set by an unfamiliar combination of properties. The intuition only holds in idealised conditions.

items.title: Twice as far doesn't mean half the gravity — it means a QUARTER
items.claim: Gravity, Coulomb force, light intensity, radio signal strength all follow inverse-square laws. Move twice as far away and you don't halve the strength — you quarter it. The geometry of 3D space, not physics, drives this.

options.text: The same total 'flux' (energy, field lines, or whatever flows outward) spreads over a sphere whose surface area grows as r^2. Intensity per unit area falls as 1/r^2 — geometric, not physical

items.reveal:
Newton's gravity: F = G * m1 * m2 / r^2.
Coulomb's law: F = k * q1 * q2 / r^2.
Light intensity: I = power / (4 * pi * r^2).
Gravitational and electromagnetic potential energy: U ∝ 1/r.

The common thread: in 3D space, the surface area of a sphere of radius r is 4 * pi * r^2. Any quantity radiating outward (energy, electric field, gravitational influence) spreads over this growing area. Intensity per unit area scales as 1/r^2.

If we lived in 2D, the analogous laws would be 1/r (intensity spreads over a circumference of 2 * pi * r). In 4D, it would be 1/r^3. The dimensionality of space is encoded in the exponent.

In fact, modern physics tests for 'higher-dimensional' theories by looking for deviations from 1/r^2 at very short ranges. So far, none seen down to ~10^(-5) metres.

Applications:
- Move twice as far from a fire: get 1/4 the warmth.
- Move three times as far from a noise source: hear 1/9 the intensity (sound pressure decreases as 1/r in spherical waves, intensity ∝ pressure squared = 1/r^2).
- Stars further away appear dimmer by 1/r^2 — leveraged for cosmic distance measurement (standard candles).
- Cell phone signal degradation as you walk away from a tower follows 1/r^n where n depends on environment (line-of-sight ~2, urban ~3-4 due to obstacles).

Kepler's third law (T^2 ∝ a^3) and Newton's gravity were unified because the 1/r^2 force law is precisely what makes elliptical orbits work — Newton's biggest mathematical victory.
items.why: The 1/r^2 pattern looks like a coincidence of physics. It's actually the geometry of 3D space showing up everywhere. The exponent IS the dimensionality.
